To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) bird species richness is higher in forest areas than in agricultural areas; (2) responses to land-use changes are species-specific; (3) forest species respond positively to landscape-scale forest cover; (4) open area species and habitat generalists respond positively to site-scale habitat complexity; and (5) the double-stranded conservation strategy, in which landscape-scale forest cover is preserved and site-scale habitat structure is maintained would benefit conservation of Madagascar's avifauna.

(1) bird species richness and composition are strongly associated with forest cover and habitat structure in a Malagasey forest-agriculture frontier, (2) frugivorous species are particularly sensitive to forest loss, and (3) the conservation of forest avifauna is likely to benefit from both a landscape-scale approach and a site-scale approach, which would involve the preservation of forest cover and habitat complexity, respectively.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of smallholder slash-and-burn agriculture on native bird species, which is a widespread land-use practice in Madagascar.
the effects of habitat structure and forest cover on the bird assemblages in a tropical forest-agricultural frontier in Madagascar.

(1) the species richness in the Ranomafana landscape is higher in forests, (2) forest species richness is positively related to forest cover at a landscape scale, while open area species richness is positively associated with habitat complexity at a site scale, (3) forest species richness was positively related to forest habitat complexity, while open area habitat species richness was positively associated with habitat heterogeneity.

the conservation of Madagascar's forest avifaunal diversity requires the preservation of both forest cover and vegetation structure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the agricultural matrix surrounding the forest is not an ecological dead zone, but a mosaic of different habitats, which are inhabited by different assemblages of species.
the agricultural matrix surrounding Ranomafan National Park in Madagascar is characterized by a high turnover in avian communities from forest-associated to open area and generalistic species.

, in Madagascar's agricultural matrix, the conservation of forest cover is of utmost importance to preserve the forest avifauna, and that the preservation of vegetation complexity is also of importance for some species.
The main takeaway from our work is that

conservation efforts in Madagascar's agricultural matrix should be directed toward maintaining the island's remaining native forest and toward preserving the habitat structure in smallholder agricultural areas.

the conservation of the island’s native birds is not possible without the preservation of the remaining forest patches, and that the agricultural matrix surrounding the forest should be as complex as possible.

, in Madagascar, the conservation of native species will depend on a dual conservation strategy, which combines landscape-scale forest cover conservation and site-scale habitat complexity maintenance, as a way of preserving forest-dependent species and their ecological functions.
